chunks: What an op-amp is and how it works. The question: What is an opamp? How does it work?
An op-amp is an amplifier with two inputs and one output. It takes the difference between the inputs and multiplies it by a huge number. On its own this is too big to be useful.
With feedback from the output back to one input, it becomes a precise amplifier whose gain you choose with resistors.
Picture someone steering a boat by watching a flag. They turn the wheel hard whenever the flag is off-center, and straighten up when it is centered.
The harder they react, the more tightly they hold the course. An op-amp does the same: it pushes the output as hard as needed until the two inputs match.
Two inputs, one output, and two supply pins. The output is the gain times the voltage difference between the inputs, limited by the supplies.
Inverting / non-inverting input: the two inputs, marked minus and plus. Open-loop gain ( A ): the raw gain, typically 100,000 or more.
Negative feedback: sending part of the output back to the minus input. Rail: the supply voltage the output cannot exceed.
Closed-loop gain: the gain of the whole circuit, set by the feedback resistors.
Without feedback, a 1 millivolts difference times a gain of 100,000 would try to make 100 volts, so the output hits a rail.
Now add feedback with R f equals 9 kilohms from the output to the minus input, and R g equals 1 kilohms from the minus input to ground. Apply 0. 1 volts to the plus input.
The output settles where the divider returns 0. 1 volts to the minus input, which is 1 volts. The gain is 1 plus 9 over 1 equals 10 . That is the whole idea.
"An op-amp is a high-gain differential amplifier: the output is a huge gain, around 10 to the 5 or more, times the difference between its two inputs.
Open-loop it just saturates, so you wrap negative feedback around it.
Then it forces the two inputs to nearly the same voltage, and the closed-loop gain is set by external resistors, roughly 1 over beta , instead of by the op-amp's own loose gain.
Inside it's an input differential pair, a gain stage with a compensation capacitor, and an output stage."
